title: Why is the Ship of Theseus a problem?
one_sentence_answer: Because two perfectly reasonable rules for what makes something the same thing over time — continuity of matter and continuity of form — disagree, and nothing in the world settles which is right.
summary: Replace a ship's planks one at a time and you never see the moment it stops being the ship. The puzzle is not about ships; it is that our concept of identity was never built to handle gradual replacement.
confidence_reason: The puzzle and the main positions are accurately and uncontroversially described. Which resolution is correct is an open philosophical question with no consensus, so the card presents the options and their costs rather than an answer.

levels.label: Simple intuition
levels.body: A ship is repaired at sea. One rotten plank is replaced, then another, and over years every original piece is gone. Is it the same ship? Almost everyone says yes — repairs do not destroy things, and there was never a moment when it stopped being that ship. Now add a detail. Someone collected every discarded plank and reassembled them into a ship. Now there are two, and each has a serious claim: the one in continuous use with a continuous history, and the one made of the original material. They cannot both be the original, because they are in two different places. So the question has no obviously right answer, and this is not because we lack information. We know everything about both ships. What we do not have is agreement on what 'the same thing' means when the thing changes gradually.

levels.label: Visual analogy
levels.body: Think of a football club. The players change, the manager changes, the stadium is rebuilt, the badge is redesigned — and it is unquestionably the same club, because what persists is an organisation and a continuous history, not any physical stuff. Now imagine the entire squad and staff leaving together to found a new club, while the old name and ground continue with new people. Which one is the club the supporters follow? Where the analogy stops: a club has an official answer, decided by a governing body, because someone had to write it down. The ship has no registrar, which is exactly what exposes the problem — much of what feels like a fact about identity turns out to be a convention we agreed on and forgot we were choosing.

levels.label: Real-world example
levels.body: It is not an academic toy. Your body replaces most of its cells over years, and yet you are held responsible for what you did a decade ago, so personal identity clearly does not track material continuity. Legal systems face it constantly: a company that changes name, ownership, staff and business is treated as the same legal person for the purposes of a contract signed twenty years earlier. Restoration raises it sharply — the Ise Grand Shrine in Japan is rebuilt every twenty years, and whether the current building is 1,300 years old is a genuine question with different answers in different traditions, which affected how such sites are treated under heritage conventions. Software has a version too: a project that has had every line rewritten still bears its name and its bug history.

levels.label: Technical explanation
levels.body: Philosophers separate two relations that ordinary language runs together. Qualitative identity is being exactly similar; numerical identity is being one and the same thing. The puzzle concerns the second, and it is generated by two criteria that usually agree and here do not: spatiotemporal continuity, meaning an unbroken path through space and time, and compositional continuity, meaning sameness of parts. The reassembled ship satisfies the second, the repaired one the first. Several responses exist. Mereological essentialism holds that an object's parts are essential, so the ship stopped existing at the first repair — consistent, but it makes nearly all ordinary objects extremely short-lived. Four-dimensionalism treats objects as extended in time as well as space, so what we call the ship is a series of temporal parts and the question becomes which stages we group under one label. Conventionalism holds that identity over time is partly a matter of how we choose to individuate, not a fact awaiting discovery.

levels.label: Expert details
levels.body: The sharpest version is the only-a and only-b problem, sometimes called the closest continuer problem: if the reassembly had never happened, the repaired ship would clearly be the original. So whether it is the original appears to depend on what happens somewhere else entirely, which violates the intuition that identity is intrinsic. Robert Nozick's closest-continuer theory embraces exactly that, holding that a thing's identity depends on whether a sufficiently close continuer exists and whether anything else is closer — accepting extrinsicness as the price of a workable criterion. Derek Parfit ran the parallel argument for persons through fission thought experiments and drew a more radical conclusion: that identity is not what matters, and that psychological continuity and connectedness can be preserved even where identity cannot be, so we should care about those relations directly rather than about the identity question. The four-dimensionalist response dissolves rather than answers the puzzle, since on that view no single stage is 'the ship' and the dispute becomes one about naming. What stays true across all of these is the diagnostic point: our identity concepts were formed for objects that persist through small changes, and pushing them to gradual total replacement reveals that they were underdetermined all along.

key_terms.plain_definition: Being one and the same thing, rather than merely being exactly alike.
Following an unbroken path through space and time, which is one candidate criterion for staying the same thing.
The view that an object's parts are essential to it, so replacing any part creates a different object.
Treating objects as extended through time, made of temporal parts as well as spatial ones.

misconceptions.myth: It is a trick question with a hidden right answer.
misconceptions.reality: It is a genuine underdetermination. Two reasonable criteria for identity conflict, and no additional fact about the ships resolves which criterion is correct.

misconceptions.myth: It only matters for artificial objects like ships.
misconceptions.reality: It applies to bodies, organisations, legal persons, restored buildings and software. Anywhere something persists through total gradual change, the same question arises.

misconceptions.myth: Science will settle it.
misconceptions.reality: Every physical fact about both ships is already known. The disagreement is about which relation the word 'same' picks out, which is a question about concepts rather than about the world.

misconceptions.myth: Saying it is a matter of convention means the question is pointless.
misconceptions.reality: Conventions have consequences — for liability, ownership, heritage status and moral responsibility. Recognising that a rule is chosen makes it possible to ask whether it is the right choice.

why_it_matters: It is the clearest demonstration that some questions resist answers not through missing evidence but through concepts that were never fully specified. That diagnosis transfers widely: arguments about whether something counts as alive, as conscious, as the same person after profound change, or as the same product after a rewrite, often have this structure. Recognising it changes the useful question from 'what is the truth' to 'which criterion should we adopt, and what does adopting it commit us to'.

historical_background.origin: Plutarch records the puzzle in his Life of Theseus, noting that the ship preserved by the Athenians had been repaired so often that it had become a standing example among philosophers of the question of things that grow.
historical_background.motivation: Thomas Hobbes sharpened it in the seventeenth century by adding the reassembled ship, which converts a question about gradual change into a direct conflict between two claimants.
historical_background.evolution: John Locke reframed identity around continuity of consciousness for persons, and twentieth-century metaphysics — Nozick's closest-continuer theory, Parfit's work on personal identity, and four-dimensionalist accounts — developed formal responses without producing consensus.

title: Why is English spelling so irregular?
one_sentence_answer: The spelling was fixed by printing just as the pronunciation was in the middle of changing, and it has been carrying borrowed words from other languages ever since without adapting any of them.
summary: English spelling is a photograph of a language taken mid-motion. The sounds moved on, the spellings did not, and centuries of borrowing added several incompatible systems on top.
confidence_reason: The Great Vowel Shift, the effect of printing and the layered borrowing are well established in historical linguistics. The relative weight of each factor and some details of timing remain debated, and reform arguments are matters of policy rather than fact.

levels.label: Simple intuition
levels.body: English spelling used to make far more sense. The 'gh' in night and light was pronounced, a rasping sound at the back of the throat; the 'k' in knight and knee was said aloud; the 'e' at the end of name was a separate syllable. Then two things happened at once. Printing arrived in the late 1400s and started fixing spellings in place, because a printed book is a permanent record and printers wanted consistency. And the pronunciation of English vowels went through an enormous shift over the following two centuries, so what people said drifted steadily away from what was written. Spelling became a snapshot of how the language sounded at one particular moment. On top of that, English borrows words constantly and usually keeps the donor language's spelling — so the system is not one system but several, layered.

levels.label: Visual analogy
levels.body: Imagine photographing a river and then insisting the photograph is an accurate map of where the water is. For a while it is roughly right; after a century the channel has moved and the photograph is a historical document rather than a guide. Printing took that photograph of English pronunciation around 1500. Where the analogy stops: a photograph is at least internally consistent, while English spelling is more like several photographs of different rivers pasted together — Germanic core words, French administrative vocabulary from after 1066, Latin and Greek scientific terms, and later borrowings from every language English encountered, each keeping the conventions it arrived with. That is why 'ch' is one sound in church, another in chemist and another in chef.

levels.label: Real-world example
levels.body: The word 'debt' is a made-up problem. It came from French 'dette' and was spelled that way in English for centuries; scholars later inserted a silent 'b' to display its descent from Latin 'debitum'. The same happened to 'island', which is a Germanic word with no Latin ancestry at all — the 's' was inserted by analogy with 'isle', a false etymology. Meanwhile 'ough' takes at least six pronunciations: through, though, thought, tough, cough, bough. Individually each is explicable by history; collectively they are indefensible as a system. The clearest evidence that spelling froze while sound moved is that the irregularities cluster exactly where the Great Vowel Shift operated, and that words borrowed after it — like 'machine' and 'police' — keep the pre-shift value of their vowels.

levels.label: Technical explanation
levels.body: The Great Vowel Shift, running roughly from the fifteenth to the eighteenth century, raised and diphthongised the long vowels of Middle English: the vowel of 'bite' moved from something like 'beet' toward its modern diphthong, and 'meet' moved from something like 'mate'. Because the shift affected long vowels systematically, the spellings that had represented them became systematically misleading in a way that is regular if you know the history and arbitrary if you do not. Caxton's press arrived in 1476, in the middle of this, and standardisation began with the London dialect and the conventions of individual printers — some of them Flemish, which introduced spellings such as 'ghost'. Consonant clusters that were pronounced in Old and Middle English were later simplified in speech without spelling following: the 'kn' cluster, the 'gh' from a velar fricative, the 'wr' of 'write'. Then Renaissance scholars actively re-Latinised spellings, sometimes correctly and sometimes not.

levels.label: Expert details
levels.body: The system is less arbitrary than it appears, and that is the strongest argument against reform. English orthography is partly morphophonemic: it preserves the identity of a morpheme across pronunciation changes, so 'sign' and 'signature', 'nation' and 'national', 'heal' and 'health' remain visibly related even though the sounds diverge. A strictly phonemic spelling would sever those connections and would also have to choose one dialect's pronunciation as the standard, disenfranchising every other — a problem with no neutral solution given that English is spoken as a first language across several continents with substantially different vowel systems. Reform has been attempted repeatedly. Noah Webster's American changes succeeded because they were modest and carried by a widely adopted dictionary; the more ambitious schemes of the Simplified Spelling Board, backed by Andrew Carnegie and briefly by Theodore Roosevelt in 1906, collapsed under ridicule and institutional resistance. Empirically, the cost is real: comparative studies of reading acquisition find that children learning English take substantially longer to reach fluent decoding than children learning shallow orthographies such as Finnish, Italian or Spanish, which is the strongest evidence that the irregularity is not merely an aesthetic complaint.

key_terms.plain_definition: A language's writing and spelling system.
A systematic change in English long vowels between roughly 1400 and 1700, after most spellings were fixed.
Spelling that preserves the visible identity of a word part even when its pronunciation changes.
A writing system with a close, predictable match between letters and sounds, as in Finnish or Spanish.

misconceptions.myth: English spelling was never regular.
misconceptions.reality: Old and Middle English spelling matched pronunciation reasonably well. The mismatch was created by sound changes occurring after the spellings were fixed, and by later deliberate meddling.

misconceptions.myth: Silent letters are meaningless leftovers.
misconceptions.reality: Most record something real: a sound that was once pronounced, or a relationship to a related word. Some, like the 'b' in debt and the 's' in island, were inserted by scholars for etymological display, in one case wrongly.

misconceptions.myth: Spelling reform would obviously be an improvement.
misconceptions.reality: A phonemic system would break the visible links between related words and would have to privilege one dialect's vowels over all others. Reform attempts have failed for reasons of coordination and identity, not only inertia.

misconceptions.myth: The irregularity does no real harm.
misconceptions.reality: Comparative studies find that children learning English reach fluent decoding substantially later than those learning shallow orthographies, which is a measurable cost paid by every learner.

why_it_matters: It is a case where the messiness is not decay but history made visible: every irregularity is a fossil of a sound change, a borrowing or a scholarly intervention. It also shows why a system that everyone agrees is suboptimal survives — coordination is impossible, the existing system carries information nobody wants to lose, and the costs fall on learners while the costs of changing would fall on everyone at once.

historical_background.origin: Old English spelling was broadly phonemic. The Norman Conquest of 1066 introduced French vocabulary and French scribal conventions, beginning the layering that continues today.
historical_background.motivation: William Caxton's printing press, established in England in 1476, began fixing spellings just as the Great Vowel Shift was transforming pronunciation, so the written form stabilised while the spoken form kept moving.
historical_background.evolution: Renaissance scholars added etymological respellings, Samuel Johnson's dictionary of 1755 and Noah Webster's of 1828 codified British and American conventions separately, and organised reform movements in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries achieved almost nothing beyond Webster's modest changes.

title: Why do 'mama' and 'papa' sound similar in almost every language?
one_sentence_answer: Because babies everywhere babble the same easiest sounds first, and adults everywhere hear those sounds as being about them and adopt them as words.
summary: The resemblance is not evidence of a shared ancestral language. It is the same accident repeating independently: the first consonants an infant can produce are the ones the words are built from.
confidence_reason: The pattern is documented across a very large sample of unrelated languages, and the babbling explanation is widely accepted. The direction of adoption — whether adults take up infant sounds or infants imitate — is supported but harder to demonstrate directly.

levels.label: Simple intuition
levels.body: Making a sound requires controlling your mouth, and some sounds are much easier than others. The easiest of all is to close your lips and let a voice out — that is 'm', 'p' and 'b'. Add the most open, effortless vowel, which is 'ah', and you have 'ma', 'pa', 'ba'. Babies produce these first, long before they mean anything by them, simply because those are the movements available to a mouth that is still learning. Adults hearing 'mamama' while holding the baby naturally take it as being addressed to them, and the sound gets adopted as a word. It happens in Mandarin, Swahili, Hungarian and Quechua alike, not because those languages are related but because babies everywhere have the same mouths and parents everywhere are listening hopefully.

levels.label: Visual analogy
levels.body: Think of the first path worn across a lawn. It appears in the same place in every park, not because the parks copied each other but because the geometry of the shortest route between two gates is the same everywhere. Words for parents are like those paths: they follow the line of least effort through the same anatomy. Where the analogy stops: paths are worn by many people over time, while these words are adopted by adults in a single act of interpretation — the baby is not naming anyone, and the adult supplies the meaning. That asymmetry is the key to the whole explanation, because it means the resemblance across languages does not require any transmission between them.

levels.label: Real-world example
levels.body: The pattern survives a startling test: it holds in languages with no demonstrable relationship at all. Mandarin has māma and bàba, Swahili mama and baba, Georgian — a language isolate — has deda and mama, and Quechua has mama and tayta. The Georgian case is the most instructive, because there the assignment is reversed: 'mama' means father and 'deda' means mother. If the resemblance came from a shared ancestor, the meanings should track the forms; instead the forms are stable and the assignment varies, which is exactly what the babbling account predicts. The pattern also survives deliberate testing: the linguist George Murdock surveyed over a thousand languages in 1959 and found the parental terms overwhelmingly built from these sounds, at rates far beyond chance.

levels.label: Technical explanation
levels.body: Canonical babbling begins around six to eight months and consists of consonant-vowel syllables, typically reduplicated. The consonants that appear first are those requiring the least articulatory precision: bilabial stops formed simply by closing and releasing the lips, and the bilabial nasal formed the same way with airflow through the nose. The vowel is typically a low central one, produced with the tongue at rest. The nasal has an additional and specific link to feeding — an infant with the mouth occupied and the lips closed produces a nasal sound, which associates it with the feeding parent. Roman Jakobson set out this account in a 1959 paper, arguing that these are not words the infant has learned but sounds the infant produces, which caregivers then interpret and formalise. The languages then embed them in their own morphology, which is why the forms take endings and tones consistent with each language while the core syllable stays constant.

levels.label: Expert details
levels.body: This class is important methodologically, because it is a systematic source of false positives in historical linguistics. Comparative reconstruction infers relatedness from recurrent sound correspondences, and nursery terms produce resemblances that arise independently in every generation, so they are conventionally excluded from the evidence used to establish language families — a discipline that proposals for very deep relationships have not always observed. The pattern also has an interesting exception structure: languages do exist where the parental terms do not fit, and the deviations tend to occur where a form has been displaced by borrowing or by taboo avoidance, which is evidence that the pressure is a tendency rather than a law. A related question is whether the direction is really adult-adopts-infant. The supporting evidence is that the forms are phonologically simpler than the rest of the lexicon, that they resist regular sound change, and that they are often morphologically irregular — all signs of items maintained by continual re-creation rather than by transmission. The wider lesson is about convergent evolution in culture: a shared constraint acting on independent systems produces similarity that looks exactly like shared descent, and distinguishing the two requires knowing which constraint is operating.

key_terms.plain_definition: The repeated consonant-vowel syllables infants produce before they have words.
Made by bringing both lips together — the 'm', 'p' and 'b' sounds, and the easiest to produce.
The same feature arising independently in unrelated systems because of a shared constraint.
Establishing that languages are related through recurrent, systematic sound correspondences.

misconceptions.myth: It proves all languages descend from one ancestral tongue.
misconceptions.reality: The opposite: these words are excluded from evidence for language relatedness precisely because they are re-created independently in every generation from infant babbling.

misconceptions.myth: Babies are saying the word for their parent.
misconceptions.reality: Early babbling has no referent. Adults interpret the sounds as being addressed to them, and that interpretation is what turns a sound into a word.

misconceptions.myth: 'Mama' always means mother.
misconceptions.reality: In Georgian, 'mama' means father. The forms are stable across languages while the assignment is not, which is one of the strongest pieces of evidence for the babbling explanation.

misconceptions.myth: The pattern is universal without exception.
misconceptions.reality: It is a strong tendency, not a law. Exceptions occur, generally where borrowing or taboo avoidance has displaced the original form.

why_it_matters: It is a compact lesson in how to read similarity. The same resemblance can come from common ancestry or from a shared constraint acting independently, and mistaking the second for the first is one of the standard ways to reach a confident wrong conclusion — in linguistics, in biology, and in any field that infers history from present-day patterns. The tell here is that the resemblance is generated fresh every generation rather than passed down.

historical_background.origin: The resemblance was noticed early and often taken as evidence of a primordial common language, a reading that persisted through nineteenth-century speculation about the origins of speech.
historical_background.motivation: George Murdock's 1959 survey of more than a thousand languages established the scale of the pattern statistically rather than anecdotally.
historical_background.evolution: Roman Jakobson's paper the same year supplied the explanation, arguing from the developmental order of infant sound production, and the account has been the standard one since. The forms are now routinely excluded from comparative reconstruction as a known source of spurious resemblance.

Why do some notes sound good together?

title: Why do some notes sound good together?
one_sentence_answer: Notes whose frequencies stand in simple ratios share many of their overtones, so the ear has fewer clashing pairs to resolve — and the rest is what your culture has taught you to expect.
summary: Consonance has a physical basis in shared harmonics and in how the inner ear handles nearby frequencies. But which intervals a culture treats as pleasing is not fixed by physics, and the evidence for that is stronger than most accounts admit.
confidence_reason: The acoustic mechanism — shared harmonics and critical-band roughness — is well measured. How much of perceived consonance is biological and how much is learned remains actively debated, with cross-cultural studies pointing in different directions.

levels.label: Simple intuition
levels.body: A single musical note is not one frequency. A plucked string vibrates along its whole length and also in halves, thirds, quarters and so on, so it produces a whole stack of frequencies at once — a fundamental plus a series of overtones above it. Play two notes whose fundamentals are in a simple ratio, like 2:1 or 3:2, and many of those overtones land on exactly the same frequencies. The two sounds overlap and reinforce rather than interfering, and the combination sounds smooth and settled. Play two notes very close together instead and their overtones sit near each other without matching, producing a rapid wobbling beat that the ear registers as rough. So part of the answer is straightforwardly physical: it depends on how much of the two sounds coincide.

levels.label: Visual analogy
levels.body: Think of two patterns of stripes on transparent sheets laid over one another. If the spacings are in a simple ratio, the lines coincide regularly and you see a clean combined pattern. Make the spacings slightly different and you get a moiré effect — dark bands crawling across the image, produced by near-misses rather than matches. Musical roughness is the audible version of moiré. Where the analogy stops: your eye tolerates moiré as a curiosity, while your ear has a specific mechanism for it. The inner ear separates frequencies by position along the cochlea, and two tones close enough to stimulate overlapping regions cannot be resolved separately, which is what produces the sensation of roughness rather than of two clean notes.

levels.label: Real-world example
levels.body: The mechanism explains why a gamelan sounds so different from a piano. Gamelan instruments are metallophones whose overtones are not whole-number multiples of the fundamental, and Indonesian tuning systems do not use the simple ratios of Western tuning — the two facts fit together, because with a different overtone structure, different intervals produce the smoothest result. Studies comparing tuning systems with instrument timbre find exactly this correspondence. Guitar tuning gives an everyday demonstration in the other direction: tune two strings to the same note and, as you get close, you hear beats slowing down until they stop. Musicians tune by listening for the disappearance of beating, which is listening directly to the acoustic component of consonance rather than to anything cultural.

levels.label: Technical explanation
levels.body: A harmonic instrument produces partials at integer multiples of the fundamental. For two notes an octave apart, ratio 2:1, every partial of the upper note coincides with one of the lower; for a perfect fifth, 3:2, every second partial coincides; and the proportion of coincidences falls as the ratio becomes more complex. Where partials do not coincide but are close, they fall within the same critical band — the frequency range the cochlea cannot resolve into separate components, roughly a minor third wide at middle frequencies — and produce amplitude fluctuations perceived as roughness, maximal at around a quarter of a critical band apart. Plomp and Levelt quantified this in 1965 and showed that predicted dissonance curves for complex tones have minima close to the simple-ratio intervals, which is a genuinely impressive derivation of musical intervals from auditory physiology. A separate proposal, harmonicity, holds that the auditory system prefers combinations that fit a single harmonic series because that indicates one physical source.

levels.label: Expert details
levels.body: The cultural half of the answer has firmed up considerably and complicates the physical story. A 2016 study of the Tsimané, an Amazonian society with limited exposure to Western music, found no preference for consonant over dissonant chords while their sensitivity to roughness and their preference for smooth over rough sounds remained intact — separating the perception of roughness from the aesthetic preference for consonance, and suggesting the latter is substantially learned. Western practice supports this historically: the perfect fourth was treated as a consonance in medieval theory and became a dissonance requiring resolution in later common-practice harmony, and the major third was regarded as dissonant before the Renaissance. Twelve-tone equal temperament, standard on keyboards, deliberately detunes almost every interval from its simple ratio in order to make all keys usable, so what most listeners now call consonant is not the pure ratio at all. Vertical harmony is also not universal: many musical traditions organise around melody, rhythm and timbre with little emphasis on simultaneous pitch combinations. The defensible summary is that roughness and harmonicity are real perceptual constraints that make some combinations easier to process, and that which of those a culture builds an aesthetic on is not determined by them.

key_terms.plain_definition: One of the higher frequencies a vibrating object produces alongside its main pitch.
The relationship between two notes' frequencies — 2:1 for an octave, 3:2 for a perfect fifth.
The frequency range within which the inner ear cannot separate two tones, producing roughness instead.
Dividing the octave into twelve equal steps, slightly detuning most intervals so every key is usable.

misconceptions.myth: Consonance is purely mathematical and therefore universal.
misconceptions.reality: The acoustic mechanism is real, but cross-cultural work finds societies without a preference for consonant intervals, while their sensitivity to roughness is unchanged. The preference is substantially learned.

misconceptions.myth: Pianos are tuned to the simple ratios.
misconceptions.reality: Equal temperament detunes almost every interval slightly so that music can be played in any key. What most listeners hear as a pure fifth is a few cents narrow.

misconceptions.myth: Dissonance is a mistake or a failure.
misconceptions.reality: It is a compositional resource. Tension and resolution depend on it, and what counts as dissonant has changed substantially over the history of Western music alone.

misconceptions.myth: The same intervals sound good on any instrument.
misconceptions.reality: Consonance depends on the overtone structure. Instruments with non-harmonic overtones, such as gamelan metallophones, work best with different tunings, and their traditions use them.

why_it_matters: It is a rare question where a physical mechanism and a cultural convention are both real, both partly explanatory, and easy to confuse for one another. Getting the division right is the interesting part: roughness is measurable and largely universal, while the aesthetic preference built on it is not. That distinction — between a perceptual constraint and the convention erected on top of it — recurs in colour, in taste, and in typography.

historical_background.origin: Pythagoras is credited with the observation that strings whose lengths stand in simple ratios sound harmonious together, tying musical pleasantness to number in a way that shaped Western thought for two millennia.
historical_background.motivation: Hermann von Helmholtz gave the first physical account in 1863, attributing dissonance to beating between partials and grounding musical consonance in the mechanics of hearing rather than in numerology.
historical_background.evolution: Plomp and Levelt quantified roughness against critical bandwidth in 1965, deriving consonance curves from auditory data. Cross-cultural research from the 2010s onward, particularly work with the Tsimané, then established how much of the aesthetic preference is learned rather than given.

title: Why do keyboards use QWERTY?
one_sentence_answer: It was designed around the mechanical constraints of a machine nobody uses any more, and it survived because everyone had already learned it.
summary: QWERTY solved a typewriter problem — and possibly a telegraph one — that vanished decades ago. Its persistence is not evidence that it is good, and the most famous evidence that it is bad turns out to be unreliable too.
confidence_reason: The mechanical origin and the lock-in argument are solid. Both the popular claim that QWERTY was designed to slow typists and the claim that Dvorak is substantially faster rest on weak evidence, and the card treats both sceptically.

levels.label: Simple intuition
levels.body: Early typewriters struck the paper with metal arms swinging up from a basket. If two arms that sat next to each other were used in quick succession, they collided and jammed, and the typist had to stop and separate them by hand. So the layout was arranged to keep frequently paired letters apart in the basket, reducing jams. That is a solution to a problem that stopped existing when typebars did — electric typewriters, then computers, have no arms to tangle. But by then millions of people had learned the layout, every machine was built with it, and every new typist learned it because that was what the machines had. The arrangement outlived its reason by more than a century, and it will almost certainly outlive everyone reading this.

levels.label: Visual analogy
levels.body: Think of a road that follows a river bend that was straightened a hundred years ago. The curve makes no sense to anyone driving it now, but houses were built along it, junctions were laid out to meet it, and straightening it would mean rebuilding everything that assumed the curve. QWERTY is that road, and the muscle memory of every typist is the housing. Where the analogy stops: a road can be rebuilt by one authority at one cost, while a keyboard layout lives in millions of individual pairs of hands. There is no committee that can decide to change it, and anyone who switches individually pays the full cost of relearning while gaining, at best, a marginal improvement.

levels.label: Real-world example
levels.body: The most-cited alternative is the Dvorak layout, patented in 1936, which places the most common letters on the home row and claims large gains in speed and comfort. It has never displaced QWERTY despite being available on essentially every operating system as a free setting — which is telling, since the switching cost for an individual is now nearly zero in software terms. The Navy study often quoted as proving Dvorak's advantage was conducted by Dvorak himself and has been criticised as methodologically unsound; later independent studies found the difference small or absent. Meanwhile Colemak and other modern layouts have small enthusiastic followings. The phone keyboard is the interesting exception: touchscreens had no mechanical constraint and no muscle memory to respect, and layouts were genuinely open — and QWERTY won there too, because people already knew it.

levels.label: Technical explanation
levels.body: This is a network effect combined with sunk investment in a skill. The value of knowing a layout scales with how many machines use it, and the value of a machine using a layout scales with how many people know it, so the two reinforce each other and the incumbent's advantage grows over time. Economists call this a lock-in equilibrium: nobody has an incentive to move unilaterally even if a superior alternative exists, because the cost of switching is borne individually and the benefit only arrives if enough others switch too. The Christopher Latham Sholes patent history shows the layout evolving through several iterations between 1868 and 1873, with the arrangement changed to address jamming, and further changed at the request of Remington. Notably, the design also reflected the constraint that the typebar basket had a fixed physical arrangement, so the problem being solved was geometric rather than about typing technique.

levels.label: Expert details
levels.body: Two popular claims deserve dismantling. The first is that QWERTY was designed to slow typists down. It was designed to reduce jams, which is a different objective — separating common pairs in the basket does not require slowing the hands, and a jam-free machine is faster overall. The second is that the alternatives are decisively better. Independent evaluations have generally found modest differences at best, and a well-known 1990 paper by Liebowitz and Margolis argued that the Dvorak advantage is largely folklore built on a self-conducted study, using the case to question how strong real-world lock-in inefficiency actually is. That argument has itself been criticised for understating switching costs, and the honest position is that QWERTY is probably somewhat suboptimal and that the size of the loss is unknown and likely small. A more interesting historical thread is Koichi Yasuoka's research proposing that the layout was shaped substantially by telegraph operators transcribing Morse code, where certain letter sequences needed to be distinguished quickly — an origin story with better documentary support than the jamming account alone, and one that suggests the design was optimised for a use case nobody remembers at all.

key_terms.plain_definition: The metal arm carrying a letter that swings up to strike the paper on a mechanical typewriter.
A thing becoming more valuable the more people use it, which entrenches whichever option arrived first.
A state where switching is individually irrational even if the alternative is better, because the cost falls on the switcher.
What it takes to move — here, relearning a skill built over years of practice.

misconceptions.myth: QWERTY was designed to slow typists down.
misconceptions.reality: It was designed to reduce typebar jams by separating common letter pairs in the basket. A machine that does not jam is faster overall, so slowing the typist was not the objective.

misconceptions.myth: Dvorak is proven to be much faster.
misconceptions.reality: The most-cited study was conducted by Dvorak himself and has been heavily criticised. Independent evaluations find small or negligible differences.

misconceptions.myth: QWERTY survives only because nobody has tried to replace it.
misconceptions.reality: Alternatives have been freely available in software for decades, and adoption remains negligible. The obstacle is the individually borne cost of relearning, not availability.

misconceptions.myth: The jamming story is the whole origin.
misconceptions.reality: Documentary research suggests telegraph operators transcribing Morse influenced the arrangement substantially, which would mean the layout was optimised for a use case that has been forgotten entirely.

why_it_matters: It is the standard example for lock-in, and it is more interesting than the standard telling, because the evidence that the incumbent is meaningfully worse is much weaker than the story requires. That double lesson is worth having: entrenched standards genuinely do persist past their reasons, and the confident claim that a familiar standard is badly suboptimal often turns out to rest on a study nobody checked.

historical_background.origin: Christopher Latham Sholes developed the layout across several iterations between 1868 and 1873, adjusting it to reduce typebar collisions before selling the design to Remington.
historical_background.motivation: Research by Koichi Yasuoka has argued that early adopters transcribing Morse code influenced the arrangement, meaning the layout may have been shaped by telegraphy as much as by mechanical jamming.
historical_background.evolution: Remington's commercial success made it the de facto standard, touch typing instruction entrenched it, and August Dvorak's 1936 alternative and later designs such as Colemak have never displaced it despite being freely selectable in software.

title: Why does food taste bland on planes?
one_sentence_answer: The cabin is drier than a desert and pressurised to a mountain altitude, which dulls your sense of smell — and constant loud noise suppresses sweetness on top of it.
summary: Most of what you call taste is smell, and both the dry air and the reduced pressure interfere with it. The engine noise adds a separate, measurable effect that has nothing to do with the nose at all.
confidence_reason: The contributions of low humidity, reduced pressure and noise are each supported by published experiments, including studies conducted in simulated cabin conditions. The relative size of each effect varies between studies.

levels.label: Simple intuition
levels.body: Most of what you experience as flavour is not taste at all — it is smell, arriving at the nose from the back of the mouth while you chew. Your tongue contributes sweet, salty, sour, bitter and savoury; everything else, the entire character of strawberry or roast beef or coffee, is olfactory. Now consider what an aircraft cabin does to your nose. The air is extremely dry, typically well below 20% humidity, drier than most deserts, and smell receptors need a moist nasal lining to work. The cabin is also pressurised to the equivalent of roughly 2,000 metres of altitude, which reduces the pressure at the receptors. Both effects dull smell substantially, so most of the flavour disappears. Then there is the noise, which turns out to have its own effect entirely.

levels.label: Visual analogy
levels.body: Think of trying to appreciate a painting through a dirty window in poor light. Nothing is wrong with the painting; the channel between it and you has been degraded in two independent ways. Aircraft food is the painting, and dry air and low pressure are the window and the light. Where the analogy stops: the noise effect is not a further degradation of the same channel. Loud sound does not interfere with smell — it changes how the tongue's own signals are perceived, specifically suppressing sweetness while leaving or even enhancing savoury taste. That is why the correct picture is not one channel being blocked but two separate systems being interfered with by three different features of the environment.

levels.label: Real-world example
levels.body: Airlines respond to this in ways you can observe. Tomato juice is ordered far more often in the air than on the ground, and experiments in simulated cabin conditions have found that its savoury character holds up while sweeter drinks flatten — which fits the noise-suppresses-sweetness finding. Airline caterers routinely increase salt and seasoning, sometimes substantially, and favour strongly flavoured dishes such as curries. Lufthansa has spoken publicly about the effect after commissioning research on it. The cleanest demonstration is the controlled experiment: researchers have fed people identical food while playing loud cabin-like noise through headphones and measured reduced sweetness ratings and enhanced savoury ratings, with no change in altitude or humidity at all.

levels.label: Technical explanation
levels.body: Retronasal olfaction — odour molecules reaching the olfactory epithelium from the back of the mouth — accounts for the majority of what people call flavour. That epithelium is coated in mucus, and odorant molecules must dissolve in it to reach the receptors, so at very low humidity the lining dries and detection thresholds rise. Cabin pressure at cruise is typically maintained around 1,800 to 2,400 metres equivalent, and reduced pressure independently reduces odour perception. Studies conducted in pressure chambers and simulated cabins have found perception of sweet and salty tastes reduced by roughly 20 to 30 per cent under these conditions, with sour, bitter and savoury less affected. The noise contribution is separate: sound levels of 80 to 85 decibels have been shown to suppress sweetness ratings and enhance umami, an effect sometimes attributed to cross-modal interaction and possibly involving the chorda tympani nerve, which passes through the middle ear.

levels.label: Expert details
levels.body: The umami finding is the most interesting because it is not merely a reduction. Studies have found savoury taste maintained or enhanced under cabin noise while sweetness is suppressed, which suggests the mechanism is not general dulling but a specific cross-modal effect — and it explains why tomato juice, high in glutamate, performs so differently from a soft drink. Airline catering has to solve a compounding problem on top of all this: meals are cooked, chilled, held and reheated in convection ovens, which favours dishes that survive that cycle and penalises anything depending on texture contrast or delicate aromatics, so some of the blandness is production rather than perception. There is also an unresolved confound worth naming: passengers are frequently dehydrated, tired and mildly stressed, all of which affect appetite and perception, and separating those from the environmental effects is difficult outside a chamber. The practical upshot the research supports is that dishes designed for altitude should lean on umami and acidity rather than on sweetness and aroma, which is the opposite of what looks appealing on a menu card at ground level.

key_terms.plain_definition: Smelling food from inside the mouth while chewing, which supplies most of what people call flavour.
The pressure inside the aircraft expressed as the altitude it corresponds to — usually around 2,000 metres.
The savoury taste associated with glutamate, found in tomatoes, cheese, meat and stock.
One sense altering another — here, loud sound changing how sweetness is perceived.

misconceptions.myth: Airline food is simply badly cooked.
misconceptions.reality: The same meal tastes noticeably better on the ground. Preparation constraints contribute, but controlled experiments show the environment alone reduces perceived sweetness and saltiness substantially.

misconceptions.myth: It is entirely about the dry air.
misconceptions.reality: Dryness, reduced pressure and noise each contribute through different mechanisms, and the noise effect operates on taste rather than smell — it has been demonstrated at ground level with headphones.

misconceptions.myth: All flavours are dulled equally.
misconceptions.reality: Sweet and salty are affected most, while savoury is maintained or even enhanced by cabin noise. That asymmetry is why tomato juice becomes so much more appealing in the air.

misconceptions.myth: The cabin is pressurised to sea level.
misconceptions.reality: It is typically maintained at the equivalent of around 2,000 metres. Full sea-level pressurisation would impose far greater structural loading on the fuselage.

why_it_matters: It is a vivid demonstration that perception is not a readout of the world but a construction that depends on conditions — the same food, the same tongue, a different answer. It also cleanly separates taste from flavour, which is the most useful distinction in the whole subject, and it shows sound affecting taste, which is the kind of cross-modal effect that is easy to dismiss until someone measures it.

historical_background.origin: Airlines noticed early that meals judged excellent in the kitchen were reported as bland in the air, and the initial assumption was that catering logistics were to blame.
historical_background.motivation: Research from the 2000s onward, including studies commissioned by airlines and conducted in pressure chambers and simulated cabins, isolated the environmental contributions from the catering ones.
historical_background.evolution: Work by Charles Spence and others on cross-modal perception then established that loud noise independently suppresses sweetness and enhances umami, which explained observations — such as the popularity of tomato juice — that humidity and pressure alone did not.
